1 Photosynthesis and the carbon cycle

1.1 Photosynthesis

Key words: chlorophyll · light intensity · photosynthesis

How plants make food

  • Photosynthesis means "making with light" (photo = light, synthesis = making). Plants use it to make their own food.
  • Plants take in three things:
  • water — from the soil, through the roots
  • carbon dioxide — from the air
  • energy — from sunlight
  • The energy in sunlight is captured by a green pigment called chlorophyll, which is inside some of the cells in the leaves.
  • The energy makes water and carbon dioxide react together. Two new substances are made: glucose and oxygen.

water + carbon dioxide → glucose + oxygen

  • Reactants: water and carbon dioxide. Products: glucose and oxygen.
  • Photosynthesis happens in the leaves of a plant.

Experiment: collecting the gas produced in photosynthesis

Apparatus — a water plant under an upside-down funnel in a beaker of pond water, with a test tube full of water over the funnel neck.

Method

  1. Set up the apparatus and put it where the plant will get sunlight. Leave it for at least one day.
  2. When plenty of gas has collected, put your hand into the beaker and remove the tube from the funnel, keeping the opening under the water so the gas cannot escape.
  3. Put your thumb over the end, lift the tube out, and keep it upside down.
  4. Let the water run out, then test the gas with a glowing splint.

What to observe — the splint relights. That shows the gas contains a lot of oxygen.

Why it is done this way

  • A water plant is used because the gas it releases forms bubbles that are easy to collect under water.
  • The apparatus is left in sunlight because light is needed for photosynthesis; without it, no gas would be produced.

Experiment: how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis

  • Independent variable: distance of the lamp from the test tube (this changes the light intensity).
  • Dependent variable: number of bubbles produced in one minute.
  • Control variables: the same plant, the same temperature, the same volume of water, the same length of stem.
  • Repeat the count three times at each distance and calculate the mean.
  • Conclusion: as the distance of the lamp increases, the light intensity decreases; as the light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases.
  • Safety: keep electrical wires, plugs and the lamp away from the water.

Why is photosynthesis important?

  1. It provides energy for all other organisms. Plants store some of the Sun's energy in carbohydrates. Animals get that energy when they eat plants, or eat animals that ate plants. A food chain shows the energy being passed along.
  2. It provides oxygen for the atmosphere. Oxygen is a waste product of photosynthesis. It is released from leaves and mixes with the other gases in the air. About 20% of the air around us is oxygen, and all organisms need it for respiration.
  • When the Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago there was almost no oxygen in the atmosphere. Oxygen began to collect once bacteria started to photosynthesise. Without photosynthesis, no animals could ever have lived here.
Questions from the book — 1.1

1 What are the reactants in photosynthesis? Water and carbon dioxide.

2 What are the products in photosynthesis? Glucose and oxygen.

3 The picture shows a lizard eating a grasshopper. Grasshoppers eat grass. Explain how the lizard relies on photosynthesis to provide it with energy. Grass photosynthesises and stores energy from sunlight in carbohydrates. The grasshopper eats the grass and takes in some of that energy. The lizard eats the grasshopper, so the energy in the lizard originally came from photosynthesis in the grass.

4 Explain one other reason (apart from food) why the lizard would not be able to survive if there were no plants on Earth. Plants release oxygen as a waste product of photosynthesis. The lizard needs oxygen for respiration, so without plants there would not be enough oxygen in the air.

1.2 More about photosynthesis

Key words: fertiliser · stomata (singular: stoma) · yield

Chloroplasts and chlorophyll

  • Chlorophyll is kept inside chloroplasts, which are inside plant cells. So photosynthesis happens inside chloroplasts.
  • Not all plant cells have chloroplasts, so not all plant cells can photosynthesise. In most plants the leaf cells have the most chloroplasts.
  • On warm, sunny days a plant can make more carbohydrate than it needs straight away. It stores the extra as starch, inside the chloroplasts, for use at night or in a season with less sunlight.
  • One way to check whether a leaf has been photosynthesising is to test it for starch.

Experiment: testing a leaf for starch

Method

  1. Boil water in a beaker on a tripod and gauze. Drop in a leaf for about two minutes — this breaks the cell membranes so iodine can get in.
  2. Turn off the flame before using ethanol, because ethanol is very flammable.
  3. Stand a test tube of ethanol with the leaf in it in the hot water. The green colour dissolves out of the leaf, so the colour change is easy to see.
  4. Dip the brittle leaf in warm water to soften it, spread it on a tile and add iodine solution.

Result — starch turns iodine solution blue-black. Parts with no starch stay orange-brown.

Variegated leaves — a leaf with green parts and white parts only makes starch in the green parts, because only those parts contain chlorophyll.

Inside a leaf

  • Chloroplasts are mostly in the cells in the middle layers of the leaf. Leaves are very thin, so light reaches those cells easily.
  • The palisade layer does most of the photosynthesis. The spongy layer has lots of air spaces and does a small amount.
  • The upper and lower epidermis protect the cells inside; a waxy layer on the surface stops the leaf drying out.
  • A vein carries water to the cells in the leaf.
  • Stomata (singular: stoma) are tiny holes, mostly in the lower epidermis. Carbon dioxide diffuses in through them, down a concentration gradient, because photosynthesising cells keep using it up. Oxygen diffuses out the same way.

Minerals and plant growth

  • Plants get minerals from the soil through their roots. They need only small quantities, but if the soil is short of one, the plant cannot grow to its full potential.
  • Farmers add fertiliser (which contains minerals) to increase the yield — the quantity of crop harvested.
MineralWhat it is needed forWhat happens if it is short
Magnesiummaking chlorophyllleaves look yellow instead of green; less chlorophyll, so less photosynthesis and poor growth
Nitrate (supplies nitrogen)converting carbohydrates into proteins, and also making chlorophyllleaves die and the plant stays small
  • Both shortages look similar, which is why they are hard to tell apart: both make the plant small and pale, because nitrogen is needed for chlorophyll as well as for protein.
  • Farmers can test the soil to find which minerals are lacking in each part of a field, and use GPS with their machinery to add fertiliser only where it is needed.
Questions from the book — 1.2

1 Use what you have learnt about diffusion to explain how carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf. The cells inside the leaf use up carbon dioxide, so its concentration inside the leaf is lower than in the air outside. Carbon dioxide therefore diffuses from the higher concentration outside, through the stomata, into the air spaces inside the leaf.

2 The cells inside a leaf produce oxygen. Suggest what happens to this oxygen. Some is used by the cells for respiration. The rest diffuses out of the leaf through the stomata into the air, because its concentration inside the leaf is higher than outside.

3 Compare the way plants obtain protein with the way animals obtain protein. Plants make their own protein, using carbohydrates made in photosynthesis plus nitrate taken from the soil. Animals cannot make protein from minerals; they must eat plants or other animals to get it.

4 It is difficult to tell the difference between a plant short of magnesium and one short of nitrate. Suggest why. Nitrogen is needed to make chlorophyll as well as protein, and magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll too. So a shortage of either mineral gives a plant with little chlorophyll — pale or yellow leaves and poor growth.

Starch test questions — a In which part of a cell is starch stored? In the chloroplasts.

b Explain why it was important to boil the leaf before the starch test could work. Iodine solution cannot get through cell membranes. Boiling breaks the membranes apart so the iodine can reach the starch inside.

1.3 The carbon cycle

Carbon and living organisms

  • Carbon is an element; its symbol is C. It is a non-metal and occurs naturally in different forms — diamond and graphite (the "lead" in a pencil) are both carbon.
  • Organisms cannot use carbon as an element. They can only use it as part of a compound. Carbohydrates, proteins and fats all contain carbon.
  • Plants take carbon dioxide from the air and use it in photosynthesis to make carbohydrates, then use those to make proteins and fats.
  • Animals get carbon compounds by feeding on plants or on other animals. Decomposers get theirs by breaking down waste products and dead remains.

Returning carbon dioxide to the air

  • Respiration puts carbon dioxide back into the air:

glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water

  • All organisms respire all the time. Plants respire at night too, when they cannot photosynthesise, so they give out carbon dioxide just as we do. Decomposers respire as they break down dead material.

Investigation: hydrogencarbonate indicator

Hydrogencarbonate indicator changes colour with the concentration of carbon dioxide:

ColourCarbon dioxide concentration
purplenone
redlow
yellowhigher
TubeContentsLight?What happens
Awater plantdark (black paper)plant only respires → carbon dioxide released → yellow
Bwater plantlightphotosynthesis is faster than respiration → carbon dioxide used up → purple
Cmaggotsdarkanimals respire → carbon dioxide released → yellow
Dmaggotslightanimals respire → carbon dioxide released → yellow
Ewater plant + maggotsdarkboth respire → carbon dioxide released → yellow
Fwater plant + maggotslightthe plant photosynthesises faster than both respire → carbon dioxide used up → purple
  • The platform is put in every tube, even those with no animals, so that the tubes are otherwise identical — it is a control variable.

Fossil fuels and combustion

  • When organisms die in places with no oxygen (a peat bog, deep ocean), decomposers cannot respire, so the bodies are not broken down. They are buried by sediment, and high pressure and heat slowly change them into fossil fuels: coal, oil and natural gas.
  • Oil and natural gas formed from tiny marine organisms that fell to the sea bed. Coal formed from plants that grew in huge swamps.
  • This takes a very long time — most fossil fuels used today formed hundreds of millions of years ago. That is why they are non-renewable: we use them far faster than they can be replaced.
  • Burning a fossil fuel is combustion: the carbon in it combines with oxygen from the air and forms carbon dioxide.
  • Fossil fuels are not fossils. A fossil is the remains or traces of an organism turned to rock, and you can still see the organism's shape. Fossil fuels look nothing like organisms.

The carbon cycle

ProcessMoves carbonEffect on carbon dioxide in the air
photosynthesisair → plantsdecreases
respirationorganisms → airincreases
feedingplants → animals → decomposersno direct change
decompositiondead remains → decomposers → airincreases
formation of fossil fuelsdead organisms → fossil fuels (very slow)decreases
combustionfossil fuels → airincreases
Questions from the book — 1.3

1 b The arrows in a food chain represent energy. Do they also show how carbon atoms pass along? Explain. Yes. The energy is passed on inside carbohydrates, fats and proteins, and all of those compounds contain carbon atoms. So when one organism eats another, carbon atoms move along the arrow as well as energy.

2 Name three different compounds in your body that contain carbon atoms. Carbohydrates (such as glucose), proteins and fats.

3 How would a carbon cycle drawn before humans were present differ from the one above? There would be no combustion of fossil fuels, so no arrow returning carbon from fossil fuels to the air (apart from natural fires). Much less carbon dioxide would be added to the atmosphere, so the amount in the air would stay roughly steady.

4 Explain why fossil fuels are non-renewable resources. They take hundreds of millions of years to form from dead organisms, but we burn them within a few hundred years. They are being used up far faster than they can be replaced.

1.4 Climate change

Key words: slush · mass extinction · meteorites · meteoroids · meteors

Greenhouse gases

  • Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases. They trap heat energy in the atmosphere and keep the Earth warm.
  • Without any carbon dioxide the Earth would be frozen and could not support life. The problem is that there is now too much of it.
  • Carbon that was locked in fossil fuels for millions of years is released as carbon dioxide when we extract and burn them. Carbon dioxide levels are rising, and this is changing the climate.

Climate change in the past

  • Climate is the long-term pattern of temperature, wind and rainfall.
  • Ice ages: the first one we know about was around 2 billion years ago. Since then the Earth has cycled between warm periods (no ice, even at the poles) and cold periods called ice ages (ice at the poles).
  • Snowball Earth: perhaps about 650 million years ago the whole Earth was covered in ice and snow. It is also called "slushball Earth" because scientists are not sure everything froze completely (slush is melting ice). The cause is still not fully understood.
  • Asteroid impact: dust thrown into the air meant less light reached the surface, so plants could not photosynthesise, food chains collapsed and animals had less food. Less heat from the Sun reached the surface, so the Earth became much colder. This caused a mass extinction — up to 75% of all species alive at the time died out, including the dinosaurs.
  • There are about 175 known asteroid impact craters on Earth. The crater in the USA is more than 1 km wide and 170 m deep, formed about 50 000 years ago.

Objects from space

TermMeaning
asteroida large rocky object orbiting the Sun
meteoroidan object in space smaller than an asteroid
meteora meteoroid that has entered Earth's atmosphere (a "shooting star")
meteoritethe part of a meteoroid that reaches Earth's surface — about 500 a year
  • Most meteors burn up because of the heat from friction with the atmosphere. Large ones can create shockwaves — in 2013 a meteor exploded over Russia and shattered windows.
  • Since 1998 scientists have made detailed observations of objects that could damage Earth. They assess the risk from the mass or diameter of the object and its closest possible approach to Earth. A more massive asteroid passing further away can be a greater risk than a small one passing close.

Climate change today and in the future

  • For the last 2000 years or so the climate has been fairly stable, which let people choose crops and know when to sow and harvest.
  • Now the mean temperature of the Earth is increasing, caused by rising carbon dioxide concentration. More carbon dioxide traps more heat close to the surface.
  • Between 1880 and 2016 the mean temperature rose by about 1.0 °C. The trend was roughly flat from 1880 to about 1910, then rose steadily from 1910 to 2016.

Impacts

  • More extreme weather. Higher temperatures mean more energy in the atmosphere, so more and stronger hurricanes and typhoons. Tropical cyclone Idai hit south-east Africa in 2019 and killed more than 1300 people. No single storm can be blamed on climate change, because storms happen anyway — but there seem to be more of them and they are more violent.
  • Less predictable rainfall. Rains may come late, not at all, or far too heavily. The 2019 monsoon in Pakistan, India, Nepal and Bangladesh came late and was heavier than usual, flooding millions of people. Long droughts also increase the risk of wildfires.
  • Rising sea levels. Water expands when it is heated, so a warmer ocean takes up more space. Melting ice caps and glaciers on land add extra water. Sea level is rising about 3 mm per year, so roughly 300 mm (30 cm) more by the end of this century. More than 600 million people are at risk of flooding, and coastal megacities such as Shanghai, Mumbai and Los Angeles are especially vulnerable.

Experiment: how rising temperature affects sea level

  • Experiment 1 — melting ice. Ice floating in the water (like sea ice) does not change the level when it melts. Ice held above the water in a funnel (like ice on land) raises the level when it melts.
  • Experiment 2 — a conical flask completely full of cold coloured water with a thermometer and a thin glass tube. As a lamp warms the water, the water level in the tube rises, because water expands when heated.
  • Conclusion: sea level rises both because land ice melts and because sea water expands as it warms.
Questions from the book — 1.4

1 Describe what an asteroid is, and where asteroids are found. An asteroid is a large rocky object that orbits the Sun. Most are found in the asteroid belt, between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

2 Outline three ways in which the asteroid collision would have made survival difficult. Dust blocked sunlight, so plants could not photosynthesise and food chains collapsed. Less heat from the Sun reached the surface, so the Earth became much colder. The impact itself destroyed habitats over a huge area.

3 How much higher was the mean temperature in 2016 than in 1880? About 1.0 °C higher.

4 Describe the trend between 1880–1910 and between 1910–2016. Between 1880 and 1910 the temperature stayed roughly the same, with small ups and downs. Between 1910 and 2016 it rose steadily, and the rise became faster towards the end.

5 Calculate by how much sea level is predicted to rise by the end of this century. About 3 mm per year for about 100 years, so roughly 300 mm (30 cm).

6 Explain why sea level is predicted to rise. Sea water expands as it gets warmer, and ice caps and glaciers on land are melting and adding extra water to the oceans.
